content.content:
# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.

The option on the table was to do the rename as its own cycle and add a backlog entry for it. Rung 3 would still add the flag as `--agent-dir`.

content.text:
Good. That settles question 1: `repos.agent` becomes `repos.agent-dir`, and rung 3's flag ships as `--agent-dir`.

`config --update` works with the rule you set on 2026-08-12. That rule has an old key name rejected with a fix-it message, never accepted as an alias. The last rename, `repos.bot` to `repos.agent`, left each user to edit their own config by hand, guided by `reject_old_agent_keys` in `src/legacy_vc_config.rs:113`. With `--update`, the command makes that edit, and the rejection message just tells users to run `vc-x1 config --update`. Normal config reads still accept only the new name. The old names get a table like `OLD_AGENT_KEYS`, and `--update` reads that table.

Some things the rename cycle would need to handle:
- **`.vc-config.md` has prose around its settings.** The update has to change only the key line inside the settings block. It must not touch the surrounding text, including references like our `[9]`. It should report any prose that still uses the old name rather than guess at a rewrite.
- **Which config files:** it needs to cover both repos' config files in one run, like the fix-it message says.
- **Dry run:** `fix-desc` and `fix-todo` show changes without making them unless told otherwise. `config --update` should probably behave the same way.
- **One table for every rename:** if `--update` reads a single table of old-to-new names, it can also fix older configs that still say `repos.bot`.

My suggestion is to make it its own cycle, **feat: rename repos.agent to repos.agent-dir, with config --update**, filed as a `## Todo` entry by this cycle. The key has to be renamed on its own anyway, and `--update` only makes sense alongside it.

Can I go ahead with rung 2's `remote.agent-repo` rename now? And questions 2 and 3, the one-line flag-name rule in `vc-config.md` and the Todo entry for "dual-repo workspace", are still open.

content.content:
The agent repo's path, relative to the config file's directory (e.g. `".claude"` in the work
repo, `"."` in the agent repo). Its presence is what signals dual-repo mode, and a single-repo
workspace simply omits it.

```toml
[repos.agent]
homes = ["workspace-code", "workspace-agent"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The agent repo's path, relative to this config file's directory (e.g. \".claude\" in the work repo, \".\" in the agent repo). Presence signals dual-repo mode"
used-by = "default_scope, scope resolution, ochid prefixes (structural)"
example = ".claude"
```

## remote.agent

The agent-repo's name on its remote, which `clone` and `sync` need when there is no agent-repo yet
to ask. Its own table rather than a `[repos]` entry: `[repos]` registers local paths and this is a
remote name, and two keys a letter apart, one a path and one a name, were misread the day the key
was drafted.

Only the last URL segment is recorded. The owner and the host come from the work-repo's own remote,
so the two repos are siblings in one namespace and a fork under a different owner resolves to that
owner's agent-repo. An agent-repo outside the work-repo's namespace cannot be reached by derivation
and is named by a flag instead, which is the [clone
takes --agent](TODO.md#clone-takes---agent-for-the-agent-repos-source) entry's subject.

An absent key means the work repo's name plus `.claude`, which is what every workspace created
before the key carries.

There is no `[remote] work`: clone is handed the work-repo's URL as its argument and git holds it
after that, so a recorded copy could only disagree with the remote the repo actually has.

```toml
[remote.agent]
homes = ["workspace-code"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The agent-repo's name on its remote, the last URL segment only, since the owner and host come from the work-repo's remote. Absent means the work repo's name plus .claude"
used-by = "clone and sync, deriving the agent-repo's URL"
example = "myproject.agent-session"
```

## family.member

This repo's name as a member of an agent-file family: the name its sibling repos know it by,
which is also its record file in the family's messages repo (`<member>.md`). Environment rather
====

- agent [[2]]

content.text:
That failure isn't from the key rename. It comes from the squash-push tests added in the last cycle, which have already landed on `main`. I got it to fail the same way by running the test under a pseudo-terminal, with this output:

```
bot: dirty: @ has changes. squash-push? [y/N]
panicked at src/squash_push.rs:933:9: squash-push: declined (got "")
```

**Cause:** `confirm` (`src/squash_push.rs:421`) only prompts when stdin is a terminal. The tests assume `cargo test` never gives them one, and their comment says so, but that's wrong: the test binary uses whatever stdin `cargo test` was started with. My validate run had no terminal, so everything passed. Yours ran in a terminal, so the tests really prompted you:
- `asking_without_a_tty_errors_rather_than_hangs` read an empty answer, treated it as "no", and failed.
- `pushs_stage_never_asks` is waiting at the prompt for you to type an answer. That's the hang.

**Workaround for now:** `vc-x1 validate </dev/null`.

**Fix:** the tests shouldn't depend on the real stdin. My suggestion is a `stdin_is_tty` field on `Context`: `Context::new` fills it from `is_stdin_tty()`, `test_ctx()` sets it to `false`, and `confirm` reads that field. The tests would then check the same code path wherever they run. The same fix would also clean up the error message on line 422, which has a run of spaces in the middle. `push.rs` checks for a terminal in four places, and none of its tests failed here. I'd look at those in the same fix.

This is work that came up outside the plan, so you pick where it goes:
1. **An inserted rung before rung 2.** I'd save rung 2's edits aside as a patch, push the fix, then bring the edits back. This is my recommendation, since until the fix is in, `validate` hangs whenever you run it from a terminal.
2. **A `## Todo` entry**, run later as its own cycle. Until then you'd run `validate </dev/null`.

143:## Suffix scheme
## Suffix scheme

The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
step without renumbering siblings.

##### fix: squash-push tests never read the terminal

Inserted ahead of the rung in flight, whose edits wait as a patch. `vc-x1 validate` run from a
terminal failed one squash-push test and hung on another, since both reached the real prompt.

* The tests assumed `cargo test` gives them no tty, and it does not: the test binary inherits the
  stdin `cargo test` was started with, which is the terminal when a person runs it.
  - `asking_without_a_tty_errors_rather_than_hangs` prompted, read an empty answer, and failed on
    the decline. `pushs_stage_never_asks` prompted at rest and waited for an answer.
  - The agent's own validation runs with no terminal, so it passed there and the gap went unseen.
* Whether a person is there to ask is now read once, into `Context`, and a test states it.
  - `Context::new` fills `stdin_is_tty` from the real stdin, `test_ctx` sets it false, and
    squash-push's `confirm` takes it as an argument rather than reading stdin itself.
  - The whole suite now passes under a pseudo-terminal, which is how the fix was checked.
* `push` keeps its own four tty checks, since no test reaches them. They move to the `Context`
  field when a test does.

"""
assert s.count(a)==1; open(p,'w').write(s.replace(a,b))
EOF

alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
  answer

A **`Ladder details`** area follows them: one subsection per rung, the closing included, headed by
the rung's exact title. Each opens at laddering with an abstract-sized intent statement (the rung's
problem and solution in a sentence or two) and completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual
delta: design points, consequences, deferrals, never a restatement of the landed commit body. The
closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out the cycle." and completes at close-out with what
closing taught, in problem/solution form, or `_None._`.

A rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title links to the rung's
subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.

A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- <cycle title> (marker)`, and the block has no
`Ladder details` area: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's
anchor ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).

## Frozen history: chores and done

content.text:
I like the idea, with one cost to weigh, and it clashes with the rules on when it can land.

**What it gets right:** the ladder now sits directly above the subsections it links to, so it works as their table of contents, and one heading does the job two did. The block also reads in a natural order: problem, solution, check, deliberation, then the steps and what each one did.

**The cost:** the ladder is also the block's status line, since it's where `(current)` shows. Acquaint reads `TODO.md` lines 1 to 60. The ladder used to sit at about lines 59 to 68, which was already on the edge of that range. Now it's at 109, after the whole Deliberation, so a new session wouldn't see which rung is in flight without a second read. One fix would be a line near the top of the block naming the current rung. Or the acquaint read could look for the `(current)` marker instead of reading a fixed range.

**The rules conflict:** the block's layout is a convention the agent-files define in four places:
- `agent-data/notes.md:140`, the "`Ladder details` area follows them" paragraph, plus the single-step case at :154
- `agent-data/cycle-model.md`, the model layout with both headings
- `AGENTS.md:156`, which lists the block's items
- `AGENTS.md:206`, per-rung step 4

Changing the agent-files says that convention work is its own cycle, and a convention idea that comes up mid-feature becomes a backlog entry, not an inserted rung. So it shouldn't ride in this fix's commit as is.

My suggestion: put `TODO.md` back to the standard layout for this rung, and file **The ladder heads the Ladder details area** as a `## Todo` entry, noting the acquaint-read cost. If you'd rather keep it now as an exception, the rules allow that if you say so, and I'd record the exception in the rung's details. Which do you want?

Separately, on the Continuation notes reading `_None._`: that's because I cleared the working copy. The notes were part of rung 2's edits, so they're in the patch and come back when I reapply it. At that point I'll replace them with the three items still open: the `repos.agent-dir` + `config --update` Todo entry, the flag-name rule, and the "dual-repo workspace" term entry.

content.text:
Honestly, nobody, not in any real sense. `TODO.md` isn't one of the agent-files, and no code reads either heading. The costs are small:

1. **The record won't match the rules for a while.** The agent-files would still describe the old layout. A later session that reads `notes.md` or `cycle-model.md` before `TODO.md` could see a mismatch and "fix" it back. A one-line note of the exception prevents that.
2. **The acquaint read.** The ladder moves outside the 60 lines a new session reads first. Since the Continuation notes name the rung in flight at every restart, this matters less than I suggested.

What the rule really protects is the agent-file text itself: changes to `notes.md`, `cycle-model.md` and `AGENTS.md` stay out of feature commits, so a convention change is reviewed on its own. Your change doesn't touch any of them.

So here's what I'd do: keep your layout in this rung and record the exception in the rung's details as covering the `TODO.md` layout only, not the agent-file wording. I'd also file a `## Todo` entry to update those four places to match, run as its own convention cycle. Is that your go on the exception?

Entries are in priority order, the first highest, and reprioritizing is moving an entry. Each is a
`###` heading, so a citation is a link to its anchor. Long-tail entries live in
[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the [Prose form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form).
Deeper detail goes in a `notes/` design file (link via `[N]` ref).

### squash-push and status take a SCOPE, and push resolves its own bookmarks

(wink, 2026-09-17) `squash-push -R .agent-session` bakes in a path the config already knows, and
the path differs by project, `.agent-session` here and `.claude` historically, so the invocation
goes stale when it moves. `vc-x1 squash-push agent` is shorter, cannot go stale, and reads as what
it means. The design, decided in conversation:

- `SCOPE` is the positional on `squash-push`, with `--scope` as its flag form, the shape
  [`status`](#status-prints-a-verdict-per-repo-and-exits-with-a-bit-per-side) already has. `BOOKMARK`
  moves to `-b`/`--bookmark`, since once the default is the line's own bookmark, naming one is the
  rare override and the rare thing belongs on a flag. This is a breaking CLI change, and the callers
  are the user and `push`'s stage, which builds params directly and never parses argv.
- `-R`'s meaning shifts from "the repo to operate on" to "the workspace root to resolve the scope
  against", which is what `status`'s `-R` already means. A second behavior change in one flag, so it
  wants saying out loud in the docs.
- `push` takes no `SCOPE`: it is always both repos, as its own help says, and a flag with one legal
  value is documentation pretending to be an option. What `push` loses instead is `[BOOKMARK]`,
  resolving each repo's bookmark the way `squash-push` now does. That collapses its hardcoded
  asymmetry, the work repo's `BOOKMARK` against the agent repo's literal `main`, into one rule, and
  retires the warning in [jj.md](agent-data/jj.md#vc-x1-push-what-it-does-and-does-not-do) against
  mirroring a work bookmark into the agent repo.
- A `trunk()` tie-break is needed before `push` can resolve. At a cycle's opening the topic bookmark
  is created at `main`'s commit, so the first push's nearest bookmarked ancestor is one commit
  carrying two bookmarks, which today's resolution refuses. Dropping candidates that are `trunk()`
  when others remain reads as "the trunk sitting coincidentally at your commit is not your line", and
  leaves a genuine tie of two topic bookmarks still refused.
- `both` on `squash-push` raises what `status` never had to answer: with the work side pushed and the
  agent side failing, what the exit code is and whether anything is undone. The instinct is no
  rollback and a bit per side, the shape the status entry already proposes.

Sequenced with **status prints a verdict per repo and exits with a bit per side**, which is already
about scope handling and per-side exit codes, so the scope resolution is written once rather than
twice. Either one cycle covering both, or two adjacent with status first.

### A squash-push test reads the live repo's bookmarks

(wink, 2026-09-20) `squash_push::tests::the_default_is_to_act_without_asking` resolves a bare
`squash-push`'s default bookmark against the vc-x1 repo the tests run in, not a fixture. At a
cycle's opening the topic bookmark sits on `main`'s commit, the resolution refuses the two-bookmark
tie, and the test fails until the cycle's first push moves the bookmark off `main`. The test should
resolve against a fixture, or check only the `yes` default without resolving a bookmark. The
`trunk()` tie-break in [squash-push and status take a
SCOPE](#squash-push-and-status-take-a-scope-and-push-resolves-its-own-bookmarks) would also clear
it, but a test should not depend on the live repo's state either way.

### Commit titles carry no scope, the declared types aside

asks a title's scope for a component name, and [Conventional-commit
shape](agent-data/prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) offers `feat(push): ...` as

# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

## A bookend

Title: `refactor: extract config loader opening`

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". Its record is the
In Progress block in TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
cycle by its title and pointing at its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".

Step 8, the description:

**Title:** `fix: squash-push tests never read the terminal`

```
Run from a terminal, `vc-x1 validate` fails one squash-push test and
hangs on another. Both tests expect squash-push's confirmation prompt
to find no terminal, but the test binary inherits the stdin `cargo
test` was started with, so from a terminal the prompt really asks.

* The prompt decides for itself whether a person is there, by reading
  stdin, so a test cannot say that none is.
  - `Context` carries `stdin_is_tty`, read once from the real stdin by
    `Context::new`, and squash-push's `confirm` takes it as an argument
    instead of reading stdin itself.
  - `test_ctx` sets it false, so every op-level test runs as if no
    terminal were attached, wherever it was started from.
* The two tests call `confirm` directly and relied on the inherited
  stdin.
  - They pass `false` explicitly, and the whole suite passes under a
    pseudo-terminal, where before one failed and one hung.
```

  alone, reporting prose that still names the old key rather than guessing at a rewrite.

  missing keys where this renames old ones. One cycle may carry both.

"""),

content.content:
##### feat: init records the agent-repo's name

Nothing records what a workspace's agent-repo is called, so every reader that needs the name appends
`.claude` to the work source, and a workspace naming it anything else cannot be found.

* There is nowhere in a workspace to record the agent-repo's name.
  - A workspace is two repos ([the dual-repo model](AGENTS.md#the-dual-repo-model)), and the
    agent-repo has a remote of its own. Where it sits locally is `repos.agent`'s answer, a path
    that defaults to a directory inside the work-repo's and may name anywhere in the tree. What it
    is called on its remote was nobody's answer.
  - The work-side `.vc-config.md` gains a `[remote]` table whose `agent-repo` key holds the last
    segment of that remote's URL. The file is markdown whose `toml` fences are the configuration
    and whose prose reaches no parser, which is [how the carrier is
    read](vc-config.md#how-this-file-is-read).
  - A table of its own, not a second `[repos]` entry: `[repos]` registers local paths, and the two
    keys a letter apart were misread at review the day the key was drafted.
  - Our own config now carries `[remote] agent-repo = "vc-x1.claude"`, the name GitHub holds this
    project's agent-repo under, while `repos.agent` puts it at `.agent-session`. The two differ
    here, which is why neither can be derived from the other.
* Every workspace that already exists records no agent-repo name, and that cannot be an error.
  - An absent key reads as the `.claude` suffix, and `validate-config` suggests the key without
    counting a finding, so an old workspace still validates clean while the suggestion spreads it.
* Clone needed the agent-repo's name before it had the config that holds it.
  - The URL derivation moved to after the work clone, beside the `repos.agent` read already waiting
    there. The legacy branch is not asked for the key, since it is reached only when the `[repos]`
    config was rejected.
* Init had the project's name and the remote's both in reach, and recorded the project's.
  - The value written is the last segment of the agent-repo's origin URL, not the plan's `bot_name`,
    which is the local directory's project name. The `cli_sync` fixture caught it: a project called
    `tr` whose agent bare is `remote-work.claude.git`.

##### feat: init defaults to .agent-session

### Workspace config tables

A work-side `.vc-config.md` holds up to six tables. `[repos]` is structural and written by `init`:
it registers the two repos' local paths. `[remote]` (0.84.11) holds remote names rather than paths,
and its one key is the agent-repo's name on its remote, which `clone` reads before there is an
agent-repo to ask. Only the last URL segment, since the owner and the host come from the work repo's
own remote, so the two repos are siblings in one namespace. An absent key means the work repo's name
plus `.claude`, the name every workspace created before the key carries. `[family]` and `[validate]`
(added at 0.80.0) hold what used to be prose in the project layer: the agent-file family this repo
belongs to, and the commands that validate it. `[agent-files.diff]` and `[agent-files.copy]`
(0.83.0) hold the defaults for the `agent-files` commands' `DIR` operand and `--custom` choice. All
six are work side only: `validate-config` reports them unknown in the agent repo's config.

````markdown
```toml
[repos]
work = "."
agent = ".claude"                 # the agent repo's directory, relative to this file
```

```toml
[remote]
agent-repo = "vc-x1.claude"       # the agent repo's name on its remote
```

```toml
[family]
member = "vc-x1"                  # this repo's name in the family, and its messages record
template = "../vc-x1-template/work"  # the payload directory holding the pinned agent-files
messages = "../vc-x1-messages"    # the family's notification repo
```

```toml
[validate]
full = [                          # the per-commit validation, in order, one command per element
  "cargo fmt",
  "cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings",
  "cargo test",
  "cargo install --path . --locked",
]
fast = ["cargo test --bins"]      # the subset a ladder rung runs
```

```toml
[agent-files.diff]
dir = "../iiac-perf"              # default DIR for agent-files diff, else family.template
custom = true                     # compare custom.md too, as -c/--custom would

[agent-files.copy]
dir = "../vc-x1-template/work"    # default DIR for agent-files copy, else family.template
custom = false                    # never copy custom.md unless -c/--custom
```
````

The `custom` keys are `bool` keys, a bare `true` or `false`: `validate-config` reports a quoted
or other value as a finding by shape, and the commands refuse a config that holds one. A `dir`
is relative to the config file's directory, and absent, the command falls back to
`family.template`. The flags win over the table for one run: `-c`/`--custom` turns custom.md
on, `--no-custom` turns it off, and a `DIR` operand replaces `dir`.

The `[validate]` lists are `str-list` keys: a TOML array of strings, one element per invocation,
on one line or spread to the closing `]`. Each element is one command whose exit status is
checked, so a command with its own spaces and dashes is one quoted string.
[`vc-x1 validate`](#validate) (and `--fast`) runs them, `validate-config` checks the tables'
keys and shapes, and `config work` prints the schema with every key's example:

```
vc-x1 validate-config                       # both sides
vc-x1 validate-config work                  # the work side only
vc-x1 validate-config agent                 # the agent side only
vc-x1 validate-config .claude/.vc-config.md # a specific file, checked against every home
vc-x1 config work                             # the work side's schema, [family], [validate], and [agent-files.*] too
vc-x1 config agent                            # the agent side's schema
vc-x1 config .claude/.vc-config.md            # the whole schema, labelled with the path
```

content.text:
You're right. The Todo entry I filed spells it `config --update`, a flag on today's `config` command, and iiac-perf has a separate `update-config` command. Some thoughts:

**1. iiac-perf's `update-config` does the job of both our entries.** "With no flags it brings an older file up to date": it rebuilds the file from the current template with the file's own values filled in. Our Todo splits that into two entries:
- `config --merge` adds keys the file is missing.
- `config --update` renames keys whose names changed.

Both are "bring the file up to date", so one command covering both is simpler. I'd merge the two entries.

**2. How iiac-perf handles an old name doesn't fit our rename.** In iiac-perf, a key it no longer knows fails with its name, and nothing renames it. Our case needs the old-to-new table, or `repos.agent` just becomes an error with no automatic fix. That table is the one real addition over iiac-perf's version.

**3. Losing prose is fine for iiac-perf and wrong for us.** iiac-perf regenerates the file and warns that the author's prose and comments are lost, with `--backup` as the fallback. Ours can't work that way. `.vc-config.md` puts its settings inside `toml` blocks in a markdown file, and the text around them is written by people and linked with `[N]` references. Our own file's text around `[9]` would be wiped on every update. So ours has to edit the setting lines in place and leave the text alone. That's harder than regenerating, and it's why the entry says to report leftover old names in the text rather than rewrite them.

**4. The name is a family question, and it pulls against a Todo we already have.** Matching iiac-perf would give the family one spelling, so a user of both tools types the same thing. But this repo has **Nest the validate and fix commands** in its Todo, which points toward `config update` as a subcommand, not `update-config` as a separate command. Either works, as long as the family picks one. I think it deserves a thread in `vc-x1-messages` to iiac-perf, not a call made here alone.

**5. `init-config` has no home here.** In iiac-perf, `init-config` prints or writes a starting config. Our `config` command already prints the settable keys, and `init` writes the file. Adding `init-config` next to `init` would be confusing, so I'd leave it out.

The plain version: iiac-perf's `update-config` is what we want in spirit, one command that brings an old config up to date. Ours has to add renaming old keys and must keep the text around the settings. I'd merge our two config Todo entries into one and settle the name with iiac-perf through the messages repo.

Here's the description for step 8:

**Title:** `feat: init records the agent-repo's name`

```
Nothing records what a workspace's agent-repo is called on its remote,
so clone appends `.claude` to the work source, and a workspace whose
agent-repo has any other name cannot be cloned.

* A workspace has nowhere to record the agent-repo's remote name.
  - The work-side `.vc-config.md` gains a `[remote]` table whose
    `agent-repo` key holds the last segment of that remote's URL, the
    owner and host coming from the work-repo's own remote.
  - It is a table of its own rather than a `[repos]` entry, since
    `[repos]` registers local paths and this is a remote name.
  - This repo's own config records `vc-x1.claude`, which differs from
    its `.agent-session` directory.
* Every existing workspace lacks the key, and that cannot be an error.
  - An absent key means the work repo's name plus `.claude`, and
    `validate-config` suggests the key without counting a finding.
* Clone needs the name before it has the config that holds it.
  - Deriving the agent-repo's URL moves to after the work clone, where
    the cloned config can be read.
* Init must record the remote's name, not the project's.
  - The value written is the last segment of the agent-repo's origin
    URL, and the `cli_sync` fixture checks it.
```

content.content:
### feat: init adopts an existing tree

#### Problem

Today `vc-x1 init` creates a workspace from nothing and refuses any target that already exists, so a
directory holding work cannot become a dual workspace. The recovery is by hand on both sides, two
colocated `jj git init` runs, two `.vc-config.md` files, two `.gitignore` files, the remotes, and
the symlink, and the two initial commits end up with no `ochid:` cross-link, since a trailer is
never hand-written. Three inputs want the one command: a plain directory that is no repo at all, a
repo with no `.vc-config.md`, and a repo whose config declares only the work side. Beside that, the
agent side a fresh init creates lands at `<project>/.claude`, the mount collision this repo left
when it moved to `.agent-session`, and the agent remote's name is derived by appending `.claude` to
the work source rather than read from anywhere, so nothing records what an existing workspace's
agent-repo is called.

#### Solution

The flag `--adopt` turns the refusal of an existing target into the upgrade. Init detects which of
four states the target is in, a plain directory, a POR, a single-repo workspace, or an already-dual
one it refuses, and grows the missing agent side: the agent-repo created and published,
`repos.agent` written, the work-side `.gitignore` given its line, and the symlink installed. A plain
directory's content becomes the work-repo's first commit, and a repo's history is left alone. Beside
it the agent side's default name becomes `.agent-session` on the directory and on the remote, with
`--agent-dir` for the directory, `--agent-repo` for a full remote name, and `--agent-suffix` for a
suffix that must begin with `.` or `-`, and a new `[remote] agent-repo` key records the remote's
name so clone and sync read it instead of deriving it. An absent key means `.claude`, which is what
keeps every workspace created before the change clonable.

#### Acceptance check

The tree at `../iiac-perf-expr-1`, a plain directory of experiment records shared with iiac-perf,
becomes a dual workspace in one `vc-x1 init . --adopt`: its `pins/` and `smooth/` records tracked in
the first commit, `.agent-session` on both sides, two public repos under `winksaville` pushed over
https, the Claude Code symlink live, and `vc-x1 status` clean on both sides. In a fixture, `--adopt`
on a POR keeps its history and adds the agent side, on an already-dual workspace it refuses,
`--agent-repo` with `--agent-suffix` is an error, a suffix opening with neither `.` nor `-` is an
error, and a workspace whose config carries no `[remote] agent-repo` still clones, taking
`.claude`. `cargo test` passes and `vc-x1 config work` lists `remote.agent-repo`.

#### Deliberation

- Two `## Todo` entries are consumed rather than one. **init turns a POR into a dual-repo** is the
  cycle's subject, and **`init` still seeds `.claude` as the agent directory** folds in because
  every adopt rung would otherwise be written against the default it asks to change, and a workspace
  adopted under `.claude` would be born into the mount collision.
  - The folded entry's open question, whether the GitHub repo suffix follows the directory, is
    answered yes (wink, 2026-09-20). Repos already published as `<name>.claude` keep their names,
    and the `[remote] agent-repo` key is what lets them.
- The plain-directory case is new work beyond the entry, which named a POR and a single-repo config
  only. Neither describes `../iiac-perf-expr-1`, and that directory is the acceptance check, so the
  third state is in scope from the start.
- The opt-in is `--adopt` rather than init detecting an existing target by itself. The entry's
  wording offered the bare `vc-x1 init .` and `notes/vc-x1-init.md` leaned the other way, and a path
  target that happens to exist should not silently change what the command does.
- Two remote-name flags, rather than one value read as a name or a suffix by its first character
  (wink, 2026-09-20). A full name goes to `--agent-repo`, a suffix to `--agent-suffix`, which errors
  unless it opens with `.` or `-`, and the two conflict. One polymorphic value would hide the
  discriminator inside a parser.
- The config key holds the agent-repo's name, not a URL. The owner and host keep coming from the
  work remote, so a fork under another owner still resolves, and `notes/forks-multi-user.md` reads
  the config as the home for repos the project already tracks and a URL as the form for a one-off
  external contributor.
- An absent `[remote] agent-repo` means `.claude`, rather than a probe of both names. Absence is
  what says the workspace predates the key, so the fallback is a fact about the file instead of a
  network guess, and it retires once the key is everywhere.
- Only init writes the key, since init writes the config anyway. A fetch that edits a tracked file
  would leave the tree dirty with an edit the user then owes a commit, so `clone` and `sync` suggest
  the key instead, and `validate-config` carries the suggestion, its job being the config files.
- The neighbouring entries stay and narrow. Both **sync clones a declared but absent agent-repo**
  and **clone takes --agent for the agent-repo's source** rank above this one: sync's act becomes a
  call into what adopt builds, and clone's flag stays the per-contributor URL the config key
  deliberately does not carry.
- The entry [repos.agent becomes repos.agent-dir, and a command brings a config up to
  date](#reposagent-becomes-reposagent-dir-and-a-command-brings-a-config-up-to-date) stays too,
  holding what was **config --merge folds new keys into a workspace config**. Adopt patches the
  `[repos]` table it owns rather than growing a general merge.
- Multi-step, with the two name rungs ahead of the four adopt rungs. Each adopt rung would otherwise
  be written against a default and a derivation it is about to change.
- The greppable stem is `init`, carried by every rung, since each changes what one command does. The
  bookends carry the bare cycle title, so the pair brackets the ladder on its own grep.
- The repos are public and the remote is https (wink, 2026-09-20), passed at the acceptance run as
  `--repo remote=` with the https namespace. The user config's ssh default is left alone, being the
  user's own file.
- The records are tracked data (wink, 2026-09-20). The 28M of `.jsonl` under `pins/` and `smooth/`
  goes into the first commit rather than into a gitignore, since the records are what the experiment
  is.
- The blocking test fix is folded into the opening rather than inserted as a rung (wink,
  2026-09-20). Publishing the bookmark is what breaks the test, so no rung could validate ahead of
  the fix, and an inserted rung would have had to push before the opening it depends on.
- The `## Waiting` entry's condition is unmet, `vc-x1 closed` not landed, so nothing promotes.

#### Ladder
##### feat: init defaults to .agent-session

A workspace init creates puts its agent-repo at `<project>/.claude`, where the harness's bind mounts
land inside the agent repo, and the name is a constant no caller can override.

  target that happens to exist should not silently change what the command does.
- Two remote-name flags, rather than one value read as a name or a suffix by its first character
  (wink, 2026-09-20). A full name goes to `--agent-repo`, a suffix to `--agent-suffix`, which errors
  unless it opens with `.` or `-`, and the two conflict. One polymorphic value would hide the
  discriminator inside a parser.
- The config key holds the agent-repo's name, not a URL. The owner and host keep coming from the
  work remote, so a fork under another owner still resolves, and `notes/forks-multi-user.md` reads
  the config as the home for repos the project already tracks and a URL as the form for a one-off
  external contributor.
- An absent `[remote] agent-repo` means `.claude`, rather than a probe of both names. Absence is
  what says the workspace predates the key, so the fallback is a fact about the file instead of a
  network guess, and it retires once the key is everywhere.
- Only init writes the key, since init writes the config anyway. A fetch that edits a tracked file
  would leave the tree dirty with an edit the user then owes a commit, so `clone` and `sync` suggest
  the key instead, and `validate-config` carries the suggestion, its job being the config files.
- The neighbouring entries stay and narrow. Both **sync clones a declared but absent agent-repo**
  and **clone takes --agent for the agent-repo's source** rank above this one: sync's act becomes a
  call into what adopt builds, and clone's flag stays the per-contributor URL the config key
  deliberately does not carry.
- The entry [repos.agent becomes repos.agent-dir, and a command brings a config up to
  date](#reposagent-becomes-reposagent-dir-and-a-command-brings-a-config-up-to-date) stays too,
  holding what was **config --merge folds new keys into a workspace config**. Adopt patches the
  `[repos]` table it owns rather than growing a general merge.
- Multi-step, with the two name rungs ahead of the four adopt rungs. Each adopt rung would otherwise
  be written against a default and a derivation it is about to change.
- The greppable stem is `init`, carried by every rung, since each changes what one command does. The
  bookends carry the bare cycle title, so the pair brackets the ladder on its own grep.
- The repos are public and the remote is https (wink, 2026-09-20), passed at the acceptance run as
  `--repo remote=` with the https namespace. The user config's ssh default is left alone, being the
  user's own file.
- The records are tracked data (wink, 2026-09-20). The 28M of `.jsonl` under `pins/` and `smooth/`
  goes into the first commit rather than into a gitignore, since the records are what the experiment
  is.
- The blocking test fix is folded into the opening rather than inserted as a rung (wink,
  2026-09-20). Publishing the bookmark is what breaks the test, so no rung could validate ahead of
  the fix, and an inserted rung would have had to push before the opening it depends on.

content.content:
### init

Create a new dual-repo project: a work repo with a `.claude` bot repo as a git submodule. Both repos
are initialized with `git` and `jj`, configured with `.vc-config.md`, and pushed to GitHub. The
bot repo is added as a submodule so `git clone --recursive` clones both.

```
# Create public project in current directory (GitHub via gh)
vc-x1 init my-project

# A URL or a path target. A slashed target with no path prefix
# (`myorg/my-project`) is refused: it reads equally as a path and
# as the retired owner/name shorthand.
vc-x1 init https://github.com/myorg/my-project
vc-x1 init ~/projects/my-project
vc-x1 init ./sub/dir/my-project

# Create private repos
vc-x1 init my-project --private

# Local bare remotes instead of GitHub (offline; used by fixtures)
vc-x1 init my-project --repo local=/path/to/parent

# Preview without executing
vc-x1 init my-project --dry-run

# Seed both repos from template directories (sibling layout)
vc-x1 init my-project --use-template \
    ../vc-x1-work-repo-template,../vc-x1-bot-repo-template

# BOT omitted defaults to the `<CODE>.claude` sibling
vc-x1 init my-project --use-template ../tmpl
# Equivalent to:
vc-x1 init my-project --use-template ../tmpl,../tmpl.claude
```

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `<TARGET>` | URL, path, or bare NAME |
| `[NAME]` | Repo directory name override (URL form only) |
| `--account <NAME>` | Pick `[account.<a>]` from user config |
| `--repo <CAT[=VAL]>` | Repo target, e.g. `local=<PARENT>` for local bare remotes |
| `--por` | Plain single repo (no `.claude/` companion) |
| `--private` | Create private GitHub repos [default: public] |
| `--dry-run` | Show what would be done without executing |

    `.agent-session`, and the URL keeps the work repo's owner and host.
  - A suffix must begin with `.` or `-` and name something after it, and the two remote-name flags
    conflict. A suffix like `-agent` is a value, not a flag.
  - The directory and the remote name are chosen apart, so `--agent-dir` alone leaves the remote
    name at its default.

  - Their configs record no `[remote] agent-repo`, and an absent key still means `.claude`, so they
    clone as before. `derive_bot_url` stays for that fallback alone.

  - The three flags are refused with it.

  since it names a template on disk rather than a workspace's directory.

content.text:
Rung 3 is ready for review. Full validation passes, all 676 tests pass, and a dry run and two refusals behave as intended from the command line.

- **Default directory:** `.agent-session`, with `--agent-dir` to name another. It has to be a single directory name inside the project, not a path, and `.git` and `.jj` are refused. The work config records it and the work `.gitignore` ignores it.
- **Remote name:** the work repo's name plus `.agent-session`. `--agent-suffix` replaces the suffix and must start with `.` or `-`; a suffix like `-agent` is accepted as a value rather than read as a flag. `--agent-repo` gives the whole name, and the two flags can't be used together. One new function, `plan_agent_side`, now works out the whole agent side for every kind of remote; before, that logic was copied in two places.
- **`--por`:** the three flags are refused with it, since there's no agent repo.
- **Existing workspaces:** unchanged. Their configs have no `[remote] agent-repo`, which still means `.claude`.
- **Tests:** the shared test workspace and about 30 test expectations moved to `.agent-session`. There are 7 new tests for the flags, and the README's init section documents them.

Also:
- **New `unwrap` sites, all with `// OK:` comments:** `plan.agent_dir.as_deref().unwrap()` in `create_dual` (set whenever the workspace is dual), and `unwrap_or_else` / `unwrap_or` in `plan_agent_side` (a missing flag means the default).
- **Stale README text removed:** the init section said init adds the agent repo as a git submodule. That design was dropped long ago, so I rewrote the paragraph.
- **Left alone:** `--use-template` still looks for the agent template in a `<CODE>.claude` folder next to the work template. That's a template on disk, not the workspace's directory. The rung's details record this.

content.text:
Here's the case for it, and I don't think it's strong.

**For keeping it:**
- **The value is always set when this runs.** `plan_init` calls `plan_agent_side` whenever the workspace is dual, and `plan_agent_side` sets `agent_dir` together with `bot_dir`, `bot_name` and `bot_url`. `create_dual` only runs for a dual workspace, so `None` can't reach this line.
- **It follows the lines just above it.** Those three lines already unwrap `bot_dir`, `bot_name` and `bot_url` with the same `// OK:` reason, and a fourth reads the same way.

**Why that doesn't hold up:** it rests on the three unwraps already there, which means one exception is being used to justify another. The rule is right to push back. A `None` here would mean a planning bug, and that should come back as an error, not a panic in the middle of an init, after the work repo is already written.

**What I'd do instead, either way:**
1. **The small fix:** `let agent_dir = plan.agent_dir.as_deref().ok_or("init: a dual plan carries no agent dir")?;`. It's one line and `create_dual` already returns a `Result`.
2. **The type fix:** replace `InitPlan`'s six separate `Option` agent fields with one `agent: Option<AgentPlan>` struct. `create_dual` would take the whole agent side once, so all four unwraps go away, including the three that were already there. That touches `InitPlan`, `plan_agent_side`, `create_dual` and the plan tests, which all already deal with the agent side's naming.

I'd pick option 2. It removes the problem rather than moving it, and it isn't much work in this code. Which do you want?

message.content: Long term I want vc-x1 to work with POR, are we making that harder or easier with what we just did?

content.text:
Easier, mostly, and nothing we did makes it harder.

**What helps:**
- **"No agent repo" is now part of the type.** Before, a single-repo plan was one where six fields happened to be `None`, and code that needed the agent side unwrapped them. An unwrap like that panics as soon as a plan without an agent side reaches it, and supporting POR means exactly that happens more often. Now there's one `Option<AgentPlan>`, and `init` picks the single-repo or dual path by whether it's set. Code for a POR simply has no agent side to reach for. The same pattern is what supporting POR in `push` will need, as **Support POR workspaces in `push`** says. Today `push` has the same kind of built-in dual assumptions that `create_dual` had. The fix there is an optional agent side that `push` checks for, where today it assumes one is present.
- **The new settings are clearly dual only.** `[remote] agent-repo` is written only on a dual workspace's work side, and `validate-config` suggests it only there. The three `--agent-*` flags are refused with `--por`. None of them adds anything a POR has to carry or ignore.
- **It helps the rest of the cycle.** `plan_agent_side` builds the agent side from the work side alone. That's what the adopt rungs need to turn an existing POR into a dual workspace: take the POR as the work side and build the agent side next to it. Before this rung, that logic was spread across two plan builders, each also creating the work side.
- **The rename helps a little.** With "agent" as the one name, it's easier to see where code assumes an agent side exists. For POR support, those are the places to find.

**One thing to watch, which we didn't make worse:** a missing `[remote] agent-repo` means "use `.claude`". That fallback only applies when the config declares an agent side through `repos.agent`, which a POR doesn't have. So a POR never gets pointed at a `<name>.claude` repo that doesn't exist. Any future code that reads the remote name should first check that an agent side exists before falling back.

The plain version: we made "no agent repo" a normal, checked case instead of an empty spot that panics when touched, and that's the change POR support needs everywhere. `init` now works that way, and `push` is the next place to do the same.

content.text:
Here's the description for step 8:

**Title:** `feat: init defaults to .agent-session`

```
A workspace init creates puts its agent repo at `.claude`, where the
harness's bind mounts land inside it, and names it on the remote by
appending `.claude` to the work repo's name. Neither can be changed.

* The directory is a constant, and `.claude` is the wrong default.
  - The default is `.agent-session`, and `--agent-dir` names another.
    It is one name inside the project, never `.git` or `.jj`, and the
    work config records it and the work `.gitignore` ignores it.
* The remote name is fixed, and derived in two places.
  - The remote name is the work repo's plus `.agent-session`.
    `--agent-suffix` replaces the suffix, which must begin with `.` or
    `-`, and `--agent-repo` gives the whole name. The two conflict.
  - The directory and the remote name are chosen separately.
  - One function builds the agent side for every provisioner, where
    two did.
* A dual plan's agent side is six optional fields, unwrapped where
  they are read.
  - The plan holds one `AgentPlan`, present exactly when the workspace
    is dual. `create_dual` takes it whole, so the four `unwrap()` calls
    are gone and its names say agent rather than bot.
* A single-repo workspace has no agent repo.
  - The three flags are refused with `--por`.
* Existing workspaces must keep cloning.
  - They record no `[remote] agent-repo`, which still means `.claude`.
```

## Test 6: `--scope=bot` on top of existing code-only workspace

`vc-x1 init repoA --repo-local=../tmp-vc-x1 --scope=bot`
(after Test 5 left a code-only workspace in place)

Expected: ideally an incremental upgrade — add `.claude/`,
rewrite parent's `.vc-config.toml` to include `other-repo`,
ochid-link the existing initial commit to a new bot-side
initial commit, create the symlink. Actual:

- Same plan-time error as Test 4 — the
  `--scope=bot is meaningless` check fires before any
  inspection of the existing workspace.
- Filesystem unchanged.
- The error message suggests `--scope=code,bot` as the
  alternative, but that path is also blocked (see Test 7).

## Test 7: `--scope=code,bot` on top of existing code-only workspace

`vc-x1 init repoA --repo-local=../tmp-vc-x1 --scope=code,bot`
(after Test 5 left a code-only workspace in place)

Expected fatal — confirmed, but at a different check than
Test 6:

- Exit 1.
- Error fires at preflight (after `Preflight checks...`):
  `'/home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/../tmp-vc-x1/repoA'
  already exists`.
- Filesystem unchanged.

## Findings: missing incremental-upgrade path

`init` today supports two and only two terminal modes from a
clean dir:

| Mode | Invocation | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Single-repo | `--scope=code` | code repo + `.vc-config.toml` (no `other-repo`) |
| Dual-repo | `--scope=code,bot` (or default) | both repos + cross-ref configs + ochid trailers + symlink |

There is **no path** to grow a single-repo workspace into a
dual-repo workspace via `init`. Both candidate invocations
fail:

- `init --scope=bot` on existing code-only → fatal at
  plan-time (`--scope=bot is meaningless at init time`),
  before any inspection of the existing workspace.
- `init --scope=code,bot` on existing code-only → fatal at
  preflight (`'<path>/repoA' already exists`).

The bot's design sketch for the upgrade path:

- Detect the upgrade case in plan-time: `--scope=bot` AND the

`init` today supports two and only two terminal modes from a
clean dir:

| Mode | Invocation | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Single-repo | `--scope=code` | code repo + `.vc-config.toml` (no `other-repo`) |
| Dual-repo | `--scope=code,bot` (or default) | both repos + cross-ref configs + ochid trailers + symlink |

dual-repo workspace via `init`. Both candidate invocations
fail:

- `init --scope=bot` on existing code-only → fatal at
  plan-time (`--scope=bot is meaningless at init time`),
  before any inspection of the existing workspace.
- `init --scope=code,bot` on existing code-only → fatal at
  preflight (`'<path>/repoA' already exists`).

  target dir contains a `.vc-config.toml` with `path = "/"`

  stay fatal — the user-facing semantics matter (does
  `code,bot` mean "ensure both" or "create both fresh"?). The
  bot's lean: keep `code,bot` strict-create (today's
  semantics) and route the upgrade through the explicit
  `--scope=bot`-on-existing form.

content.text:
Rung 4 is ready for review. Full validation passes.

- **`--adopt`** is a new flag on `init`. Init now reads what the target holds before it creates anything. The new file `src/init/adopt.rs` has a `TargetState` enum with five values (`Absent`, `PlainDir`, `Por`, `SingleRepo`, `Dual`) and `detect_target_state`, which checks for `.git`/`.jj` and reads the config's `repos.agent`. A dual workspace's agent repo declares `agent = "."`, so it counts as dual.
- **`check_target_state`** decides what happens next, and it replaces the old flat "already exists" message:
  - An existing target without `--adopt` is refused with its state named, and the message points at `--adopt`.
  - A dual workspace is refused either way.
  - `--adopt` on a missing directory is refused.
  - The three states adopt will take say "adopt does not take yet" until rungs 5 and 6 land.
- **Targets that fit no state are errors:** a file, a config with no repo next to it, or a config with no `repos.work`. An old-format config gets its existing fix-it message.
- **`--adopt` with `--por`** is refused.
- **Tests:** there are 4 new ones, for detection, those error cases, the refusal cases, and `--adopt` with `--por`. I ran the messages against a plain directory, a missing one, this workspace, and its `.agent-session`.

Choices to check:
1. **No "inside another repo" check.** I wrote one and took it out: it would block every adopt for anyone whose home directory is a git repo. The case that matters, adopting a dual workspace's agent repo, is already caught by its config.
2. **`--adopt` on a missing target is refused**, not treated as a normal create. A missing directory is more likely a typo than a request.
3. **A folder with `.git` or `.jj` counts as a repo.** Whether a git-only POR also needs `jj git init --colocate` is for rung 6.
4. **The README doesn't mention `--adopt` yet.** I'll document it in rung 5, when it first does something.

There are no new `unwrap()` calls outside tests.

content.text:
I think you're right for this repo. The measurements back it up:

| | after an edit | nothing changed |
|---|---|---|
| `validate --fast` | 5.5 s | 3.7 s |
| `validate` (full) | 9.6 s | 5.7 s |

Fast saves about 4 seconds, and it misses things. It runs only `cargo test --bins`, so it skips clippy and the `tests/cli_*.rs` integration tests. In rung 3, fast passed and only the full run caught the clippy `err_expect` failure. Since full has to run before every push anyway, fast mostly means problems turn up later.

The rules give a second reason for fast: the full run's `cargo fmt` rewrites files while a review is in progress. In practice that has helped. It only reformats code the reviewer is about to read anyway, and in a jj working copy the reformatting just shows up in the diff. Its other side effect, installing `vc-x1-dev` mid-review, doesn't hurt anything during a cycle.

**What I'd keep:** the `--fast` flag in `vc-x1` and the `[validate] fast` setting. They cost nothing, and another adopter whose full run takes minutes, say a benchmark suite, may really need them. What should go is the rule that tells the agent to use fast. That's in the agent-files: step 5 of the per-rung flow in `AGENTS.md` ("use `--fast` while a review iterates"), the Local ladders section, and its counterpart in `jj.md`.

That's a convention change, so under the rules on changing the agent-files it's either:
1. **A Todo entry for an `agent-files` cycle** that makes full validation the rule everywhere and leaves `--fast` as an option a project can use for a slow suite. This is my suggestion, since the reasoning isn't specific to vc-x1.
2. **A `custom.md` override now**, saying the agent always runs full validation in this project and naming the section it replaces. That takes effect right away, but it's a rule for this project only.

The plain version: fast saves about 4 seconds and skips the checks that actually caught a problem, so the agent should stop using it here. The flag can stay for projects that need it. Which do you want, the Todo entry, the `custom.md` override, or both?

content.text:
Here's the description for step 8:

**Title:** `feat: init adopt detects the target's state`

```
Init refuses any existing target with one message, whatever it holds,
so a directory that could become a dual workspace is told nothing
about how. Separately, this repo's quick validation skips the checks
that catch its failures.

* Init cannot tell what an existing target holds.
  - `--adopt` asks init to grow an existing target into a dual
    workspace, and init reads which state the target is in first: a
    plain directory with no repo, a repo with no workspace config, a
    single-repo workspace, or a dual-repo workspace.
  - A file, a config with no repo beside it, and a config with no
    `repos.work` are errors rather than a state.
* The refusal does not say what would work.
  - Without `--adopt`, an existing target is refused by its state and
    pointed at `--adopt`.
  - A dual workspace is refused either way, and `--adopt` on a target
    that does not exist is refused, as is `--adopt` with `--por`.
  - The states adopt will take are refused by name until they land.
* `validate --fast` runs `cargo test --bins` alone, skipping clippy
  and the integration tests, to save about four seconds.
  - This repo's `[validate] fast` is the same list as `full`, on trial.
```

questions.question: How should adopt's first commit treat files over jj's 1MiB new-file limit?

options.label: Lift the limit (Recommended)
options.description: Adopt's first commit tracks everything not gitignored, whatever its size, and lists the files over 1MiB so the user sees them. You adopted the directory, so its content is the commit; a .gitignore is how to keep something out.

options.label: Refuse and list
options.description: Adopt stops before committing and lists files over the limit; the user gitignores them or raises snapshot.max-new-file-size in their jj config, then reruns.

options.label: Honor jj's limit, warn
options.description: Commit what fits and warn with the list of skipped files, left untracked in the working copy. Fails the acceptance check as written.

     - retry with short backoff around the bookmark-set

It checks the large file is committed, the log isn't, the `.gitignore` gains `/.agent-session`, both bare remotes exist, `[remote] agent-repo` is recorded, and the trailer is cross-linked. Three smaller tests cover the refusals and a `.gitignore` that already has the line.

Rung 5 is the feature, and rung 7 was planned as its lasting test coverage. Most of that coverage has now landed in rung 5.

When the cycle opened, rung 7's stated problem was: "The adopt paths are exercised by hand on one real directory and by nothing that runs again." The plan was to build adopt in rungs 5 and 6, check it by hand on `../iiac-perf-expr-1`, and then add repeatable tests in rung 7.

Rung 5 didn't wait for that. It already carries repeatable tests of the plain-directory path: large files, `.gitignore` handling, both remotes, the recorded `[remote] agent-repo`, the cross-linked trailers, and the refusals. So rung 7's problem is mostly solved for plain directories, and rung 6 would carry its own tests the same way.

What rung 7 could still add is coverage one level up. Rung 5's tests call `init()` in-process with `create_symlink = false`. They never run the binary, and they skip the symlink step. `tests/cli_init.rs` already runs the real `vc-x1 init` as a subprocess with `HOME` pointed at a temp directory, so the symlink lands somewhere harmless. A CLI test there would cover the whole thing end to end: argument parsing, the state check, the symlink, and the final output.

So rung 7 can go one of two ways:
1. **Narrow it to the CLI test**, renamed to something like "test: init adopt runs end to end", covering a plain directory and a POR through the binary with `HOME` redirected. It would be the one repeatable check of the symlink step, which the sandbox keeps me from running by hand. This is my suggestion.
2. **Drop it.** Rungs 5 and 6 carry their own tests, and the closing's acceptance run on `../iiac-perf-expr-1` covers the symlink by hand. That's one fewer rung, but the symlink step is never checked by a test that runs again.

content.text:
Yes. `vc-x1-dev` is this cycle's build, version 0.84.12-5, and its `init -h` lists `--adopt` along with the `--agent-*` flags. `vc-x1` is the last landed release, 0.84.11, which doesn't have them. It becomes the new version when the cycle lands.

What `vc-x1-dev init --adopt` handles at this rung:
- **A plain directory (no repo): yes.** Everything rung 5 built.
- **A repo, POR or single-repo workspace: not yet.** It refuses with "which adopt does not take yet" until rung 6.
- **A dual workspace or a missing directory: refused**, by design.

Before you run it on real data, keep in mind that a real run publishes. With no `--repo`, init runs `gh repo create` under your default account, public unless you pass `--private`, and it installs the Claude Code symlink. Some safe ways to try it first:

```
# See the plan without doing anything
vc-x1-dev init ../iiac-perf-expr-1 --adopt --dry-run

# A real run on a scratch copy with local bare remotes, nothing on GitHub
cp -r ../iiac-perf-expr-1 /tmp/adopt-try
vc-x1-dev init /tmp/adopt-try --adopt --repo local=/tmp/adopt-bares
```

The second one still installs a symlink under `~/.claude/projects/` for `/tmp/adopt-try`. Remove it after you look.

The real run on `../iiac-perf-expr-1` is the cycle's acceptance check, with public repos under `winksaville` over https as agreed. It needs `--repo remote=https://github.com/winksaville`, since your user config defaults to ssh. We planned it for the closing, but it works now if you'd rather try it early.

content.text:
No. `--repo local=<dir>` isn't `repos.work`. They're two different things with confusable names:

- **`repos.work`** is a setting in the workspace's `.vc-config.md`: the work repo's own local path, relative to that config file. On the work side it's always `"."`.
- **`--repo local=<dir>`** picks where the remotes live. `--repo` has two built-in categories:
  - `remote=<URL prefix>` puts the remotes on a server, e.g. `https://github.com/winksaville`.
  - `local=<dir>` puts them on this machine as bare git repos under `<dir>`, standing in for GitHub. It's meant for tests and offline use.

  So `<dir>` is the parent directory of the origins. The work repo itself still goes where TARGET says. For a dual workspace that gives:

  ```
  <dir>/remote-work.git                  origin of the work repo
  <dir>/remote-work.agent-session.git    origin of the agent repo
  ```

  and `<dir>/remote.git` for `--por`.

"local" means "remotes on the local filesystem", which is easy to misread as the local repo. That was the source of the confusion.

On creating it: yes, init should `mkdir -p` `<dir>`. It's a directory init is told to put things in, the same way it creates TARGET's parent.

One more oddity from reading `plan_local`: the bare names are fixed, `remote-work.git` whatever the project is called. Two projects given the same `<dir>` would collide, and init refuses the second because the bare "already exists". Naming them after the project (`<dir>/<name>.git`, `<dir>/<name>.agent-session.git`) would fix that, but the test fixtures and `tests/cli_sync.rs` rely on the `remote-work` names, so that change is bigger.

Where should these go?
1. **Creating `<dir>`**: a few lines in init's preflight. It could ride in rung 5 like the step numbering, or be its own entry.
2. **The fixed bare names**: I'd file this as a Todo, since it changes the fixture layout.

content.text:
You're right that the names are the problem. I'd fix it by renaming the category, not going back to two flags.

**Why two flags already went away:** vc-x1 had `--repo-remote` and `--repo-local` before 0.41.1, and they were merged into `--repo CAT[=VAL]` on purpose. The merge made the choice config-driven. Each account in your user config names a default category and a value for each one:

```toml
[account.home]
repo.default         = "remote"
repo.category.remote = "git@github.com:winksaville"
repo.category.local  = "~/test-fixtures"
```

So `vc-x1 init foo` with no `--repo` goes to your default, and `--repo local` alone looks up its directory. Two separate flags would each need their own setting and their own rule about which one wins. The single flag with categories is what makes the account setup work.

**Why "test" isn't quite right either:** what the category actually does is have init create bare git repos in a directory and push to them. Tests use that most, but so would an offline setup, a NAS or a USB drive. Its difference from `remote=` isn't "test versus real". `remote=` expects the remote to already exist or to be created by `gh`, while this one has init make the bare repos.

**My suggestion:** rename the built-in category from `local` to `bare`:

```
vc-x1 init foo --repo remote=https://github.com/winksaville
vc-x1 init foo --repo bare=/tmp/remotes
```

"bare" says what init makes there and can't be mistaken for the work repo. Following the rule you set for renames on 2026-08-12, `local` would be rejected with a fix-it message, not kept as an alias. The same goes for a user config's `repo.category.local`, and `repo.default = "local"`, and the future config-update command could apply the rename.

Two changes belong with it:
- **Create `<dir>`** when it doesn't exist.
- **Name the bares after the project:** `<dir>/foo.git` and `<dir>/foo.agent-session.git`, not the fixed `remote-work.git`. Then one `<dir>` can hold several projects' remotes, the way a GitHub account holds several repos.

It changes the command-line interface, user configs, test fixtures and `tests/cli_sync.rs`, so it's a cycle of its own. I'd file it as a `## Todo` entry and leave it out of this cycle. Should I file it, and do you want `bare` as the name?

content.text:
Yes, that's right, and it's a good objection to my suggestion. A bare repo has a `.git` directory's contents and no working tree or index, so nothing is checked out. It's what every remote is, and GitHub stores repos that way. So "bare" doesn't set the two categories apart: `remote=` points at bare repos too. The difference is where they are and who creates them:

- `remote=<prefix>` is a URL. The repos live on a server, created by `gh repo create` for GitHub, or they must already exist for another host.
- `local=<dir>` is a directory on this machine, and init creates the bare repos in it itself.

So the name should say "on the filesystem", not "bare". Some options:
- `--repo dir=<parent>`: the remotes go in this directory. It's short and hard to misread.
- `--repo path=<parent>`: the same idea. It pairs with `remote=`, where the value is a URL prefix and here it's a path.

My pick is `dir=`, since the value is literally the directory the remotes go in.

There's a wrinkle with any name: `remote=` already accepts a path prefix. It then expects bare repos someone created in advance (the "external pre-existing" case). So "path versus URL" isn't the real split either. The real split is who creates the remotes: `gh`, nobody (they already exist), or init. Since the name is still open, I'd write the Todo entry around that distinction and leave the name for its cycle to decide:

**Name the category for remotes init creates on disk**
- `local=` reads as the local work repo. Rename it, with `dir=` suggested, and reject `local` with a fix-it message.
- Create the directory when it's missing.
- Name the bare repos after the project, not `remote-work`.
- Settle how it relates to `remote=` with a path prefix, which also means repos on disk, created by someone else.

content.text:
Here's the updated description for step 8. It now includes the step numbering:

**Title:** `feat: init adopt takes a plain directory`

```
`--adopt` refuses a plain directory as not taken yet, so a directory of
work that is no repo still cannot become a dual workspace, and init's
narration numbers its steps apart from the order they run.

* A plain directory cannot be adopted.
  - Init creates both repos around it as a fresh init would, and the
    work repo's first commit is everything its `.gitignore` does not
    exclude.
  - A directory already holding the agent directory is refused before
    anything is written, and `--use-template` is refused with
    `--adopt`, since a template would overwrite files of the same name.
* jj leaves a new file over its size limit out of a snapshot, and the
  facade dropped the report that said so.
  - The snapshot returns what it left out for size, and the initial
    commit tracks every file whatever its size and lists the ones over
    the limit. The remaining callers are a filed bug.
* An adopted directory may already have a `.gitignore`.
  - It is kept, and given the agent directory's line when it lacks it.
* A run prints steps 7, 8, 7, 9, 11 and prose for the rest, and the
  dry run lists a retired design's eleven, a `git clean -xdf` among
  them.
  - One list names the steps a plan runs, numbered 1 to N in run order.
    The dry run prints it whole and the real run prints each step as it
    starts, so the two cannot disagree.
```

questions.question: The POR already has history and usually an origin. What does adopt do on the work side?

options.label: Commit locally, push nothing (Recommended)
options.description: Adopt adds one new commit on top of the POR's working copy: `.vc-config.md`, the `.gitignore` line, and an ochid trailer to the agent's first commit. It moves no bookmark and pushes nothing on the work side; the user lands it as they would any change. The agent side is created and published as usual, its URL derived from the work repo's origin.

options.label: Commit and push to the trunk
options.description: Same commit, then move the POR's trunk bookmark (main or master) onto it and push to origin. One command finishes the job, but it rewrites the published trunk's tip without review.

options.description: Stop before writing anything and say so; the user commits or stashes first. Otherwise their work would end up inside adopt's commit.

options.label: Commit them separately first
options.description: Snapshot the user's changes into their own commit, then add adopt's commit on top.
